raw_case_text:
A 32-year-old human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-negative male patient was referred to our unit with a 2-week history of bilateral flank pain and nausea. He was found to have gross bilateral hydroureter and hydronephrosis and a blood serum urea level of 87.5 mmol/l, creatinine 1840 mumol/l and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 3 ml/min/1.73 m2. No significant post micturition residual bladder volume that would suggest a bladder outlet obstruction was noted on ultrasound. The history was further unremarkable, with no prior hematuria, lower urinary tract symptoms, surgical procedures, urolithiasis, or previous urinary tract infections. The clinical examination found him afebrile and normotensive with mild bilateral loin tenderness. Specimens for urinalysis and culture revealed no evidence of urinary tract infection, tuberculosis or schistosomiasis.
Urgent hemodialysis was commenced, and a cystoscopy noted extensive cystic and nodular lesions involving most of the bladder urothelium, but especially prominent at the trigone and bladder neck. The ureteric orifices could not be visualized, and retrograde stenting proved impossible. Biopsies of the abnormal bladder urothelium noted multiple foci of CCEG (Figure 1) and no evidence of dysplasia, malignancy, tuberculosis, or schistosomiasis.
Bilateral percutaneous nephrostomies were inserted forthwith, and bilateral anterograde pyelography revealed distended ureters with complete obstruction at the level of both vesicoureteral junctions (Figure 2). No filling defects suggestive of concomitant ureteritis cystica were noted. At this stage, our management plan was to continue dialysis with the bilateral percutaneous nephrostomies in situ and allow time for the CCEG, generally regarded as self-limiting, to resolve. Computed tomography (CT) cystogram showed a good capacity bladder, with no evidence of pelvic lipomatosis (Figure 3).
Repeat cystoscopy 6 weeks later did show a marked improvement, with bladder lesions now limited only to the bladder neck and trigone. Careful resection of the remaining lesions on the trigone exposed slit-like ureteric orifices (Figure 4), but unfortunately, these orifices could not be catheterised. Repeat anterograde pyelography showed no resolution of the complete obstruction at the lower extent of both ureters.
The patient's serum renal function showed no improvement despite the decompressing effect of the bilateral percutaneous nephrostomies. Seeing that follow-up cystoscopy showed resolution of the macroscopic cystic and nodular lesions in the bladder and no lesions requiring re-resection, a multidisciplinary decision was made to continue hemodialysis and place our patient on a waiting list for a renal transplant.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old HIV-negative man presented with a 2-week history of bilateral flank pain and nausea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was referred with a 2-week history of bilateral flank pain and nausea and was found to have severe acute kidney injury with gross bilateral hydroureteronephrosis.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV-negative with an unremarkable past medical and surgical history; denied prior hematuria, lower urinary tract symptoms, urolithiasis, surgical procedures, or urinary tract infections.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for nausea; denied hematuria or lower urinary tract symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile and normotensive with mild bilateral loin tenderness.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission blood tests showed severe renal failure with serum urea 87.5 mmol/L, creatinine 1840 mcmol/L, and eGFR 3 mL/min/1.73 m2. Renal/bladder ultrasound demonstrated gross bilateral hydroureter and hydronephrosis without significant post-void residual bladder volume. Urinalysis and urine cultures were negative for bacterial UTI, tuberculosis, and schistosomiasis.
objective.advanced_workup: Cystoscopy revealed extensive cystic and nodular lesions across the bladder urothelium (most prominent at the trigone and bladder neck) obscuring both ureteric orifices and preventing retrograde stenting. Bladder biopsy histopathology demonstrated multiple foci of cystitis cystica et glandularis (CCEG) without dysplasia, malignancy, tuberculosis, or schistosomiasis. Bilateral percutaneous nephrostomies with antegrade pyelography showed distended ureters with complete bilateral vesicoureteral junction (VUJ) obstruction and no ureteritis cystica. CT cystogram showed normal bladder capacity without pelvic lipomatosis. Repeat cystoscopy and transurethral resection at 6 weeks showed marked regression of bladder lesions (exposing slit-like, uncatheterizable ureteric orifices), while repeat antegrade pyelography confirmed persistent complete bilateral distal ureteric obstruction.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed florid cystitis cystica et glandularis (CCEG) causing irreversible bilateral vesicoureteral junction obstruction and end-stage renal disease (with schistosomiasis, tuberculosis, pelvic lipomatosis, and urothelial malignancy excluded). Despite urgent hemodialysis, bilateral percutaneous nephrostomy decompression, and macroscopic resolution of bladder CCEG lesions following transurethral resection, renal function did not recover and persistent VUJ obstruction required maintenance hemodialysis and listing for renal transplantation.
